method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-02.
questions: How do trust, reliance, actual trustworthiness, evidence, and warranted distrust interact?

used_for: Reasons to trust and reasons for a belief

evidence.excerpt: It is important because it allows us to depend on others—for love, for advice, for help with our plumbing, or what have you—especially when we know that no outside force compels them to give us these things.
Leaving the danger of trust aside, one could also ask whether trust is warranted in the sense of being plausible.

To illustrate how each of these matters is relevant, note that trust is warranted, that is, plausible, again, only if the conditions required for trust exist (e.g., some optimism about one another’s ability).
For instance, trust may not be the sort of attitude that one can will oneself to have without any evidence of a person’s trustworthiness.
The assumption going forward therefore is that the dominant paradigm is interpersonal.
Trust is an attitude we have towards people whom we hope will be trustworthy, where trustworthiness is a property not an attitude.
For most philosophers, trust is a kind of reliance although it is not mere reliance (Goldberg 2020).
Included at the end is some discussion about the nature of distrust.
One might think that if one is relying while trusting—that is, if trust is a species of reliance—then accepted vulnerability would not be essential for trust.
Annette Baier writes that “trusting can be betrayed, or at least let down, and not just disappointed” (1986: 235).

To illustrate this type of trust, consider parents who trust their teenagers with the house or the family car, believing that their [children] may well abuse their trust, but hoping by such trust to elicit, in the fullness of time, more responsible and responsive trustworthy behaviour.
Writings on this topic obviously bear on the issue of when trust is warranted (i.e., justified).
People can get into serious trouble by distrusting when they ought not to, rather than just by trusting when they ought not to.
This section focuses on the epistemology of trust generally rather than on trust in testimony specifically.
For example, if I trust my brother not to harm anyone, I will resist the truth of any evidence to the contrary.

Many philosophers respond to the skepticism about the rationality of trust by saying that rationality, when applied to trust, needs to be understood differently than it is in each of the skeptical points above.
Or it could be internalist without requiring that we have done the evidence gathering just discussed.
Although trust is paradigmatically a relation that holds between two individuals, forces larger than those individuals inevitably shape their trust and distrust in one another.
We need such a stance because we can’t always stop to reflect carefully on when to trust (i.e., assuming that some rational reflection is required for trusting well).
Whichever epistemology of trust we choose, it ought to be sensitive to the tension that exists between trusting somebody and rationally reflecting on the grounds for that trust.

sources.annotation: Distinguishes trust from reliance, justification from actual trustworthiness, and interpersonal judgment from the surrounding social climate.

evidence.excerpt: When it comes to the various ways we rely on others as we engage in the pursuit of truth, testimony is paradigmatic.

Those who deny that testimony is a basic source of justification hold that testimony-based beliefs are justified only if the audience has adequate independent reasons to regard the speaker’s testimony as trustworthy.

Such a view, known as “anti-reductionism,” was defended by Thomas Reid (1764/1983), who argued that honesty (in speakers) and credulity (in audiences) are as much a part of our natural psychological endowment, and so are as worthy of being relied upon in belief-formation, as is the faculty of perception.

In addition to the question of whether testimony is a basic source of justification, a second question concerns whether we can specify the conditions on justified testimony-based belief in individualistic terms, that is, terms that are restricted to materials from the audience alone (the evidence in her possession, the reliability of her faculties, etc.).
Still, anti-individualistic views remain controversial (see Gerken 2012, Leonard 2016, 2018).
A question that has recently begun to attract more attention from social epistemologists concerns the role of technology in testimony.

sources.annotation: Surveys testimony, group belief, aggregation, networks, institutions, misleading content, and epistemic dysfunctions; empirical model results are distinguished from general prescriptions.
